brief.notification_title: Brent $117 into Fed week: stay patient, own producers
brief.market_summary: US stocks ended a choppy week slightly lower on Friday. The S&P 500 closed at 7,623.68 (−0.52%), the Dow at 52,215 (−1.23%) and the Nasdaq at 25,955 (−0.21%). Fear of a renewed US–Iran conflict pushed Brent to a $116.72 settle, its highest close since 29 April and up 6.2% on the week. Treasuries still rallied on the week: the 10Y ended near 4.99%, down 11bp, as weak consumer data and recession talk outweighed the inflation risk from oil. Crypto is soft. BTC is holding about $80.5K after a weekend dip to ~$79.3K, while ETH ($2,340) and most alt L1s keep losing ground on ETF outflows. This week packs a Fed decision, Q3 GDP, September PCE, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon earnings, and the big oil majors' results into five days.
brief.since_last:
The last brief went out before Friday's US close. Since then:
- **Friday's close:** the Dow fell 1.23% as selling hit staples (XLP −1.92%), industrials (XLI −1.27%) and financials (XLF −1.32%). Tech (XLK +0.49%) and semis (SMH +0.74%) bounced.
- **Brent:** settled at $116.72 (+3.14%) after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
- **UMich final October:** sentiment 48.0, better than the 46.3 expected. Inflation expectations rose: 1-year to 4.7%, 5–10-year to 3.5%.
- **Earnings:** AmEx beat on EPS but missed slightly on revenue and announced ~5% job cuts; shares fell ~3%. SLB beat on EPS and revenue.

Over the weekend:
- Trump said strikes on Iran could come "today" (n41).
- Fujairah has resumed oil loadings after the attack (n17).
- BTC briefly fell below $80K (n15) amid $436M of liquidations, then recovered.
- Ethereum developers postponed the 26 Oct Hoodi testnet upgrade.

Data cautions:
- Several weekend Stocktwits/StoneX headlines are recycled from earlier dates and don't match current conditions ("record close", "after Fed rate hike", "cooler inflation": n20, n74, n77, n111, n124). Ignore them.
- The price snapshot shows Brent at $111.70 (−1.30%). That is almost certainly the next contract month, not the front month that settled at $116.72; BNO's +3.02% on Friday supports the up day.
- I don't have an official Friday close for the 10Y beyond the snapshot (4.988%; Treasury par curve 5.00%).

economic_data.takeaway: The headline beat only because the preliminary reading was so weak; it is still the lowest since May and the second-lowest on record. The part that matters is inflation expectations rising to 4.7% and 3.5%, which hands the Fed a reason to keep a tightening bias even as consumers weaken. That is a stagflation mix: bad for discretionary stocks and a cap on how far long yields can fall.
A second look at the consumer under $100+ oil. A reading well below 80 would add to recession worries (Moody's puts the odds at 50%, n88) and support Treasuries over cyclicals.

economic_data.release: FOMC rate decision, statement and press conference
economic_data.expected: Hold at 3.75-4.00% (94/100 in a Reuters poll; CME ~10% hike odds)
economic_data.takeaway: The market expects a hawkish pause (n53). What moves prices is whether Chair Warsh keeps a December hike on the table and how many members dissent in favour of a hike (Hammack, Logan and Kashkari are candidates). A clear tightening bias would push up 2-5Y yields and hurt long-duration tech just as MSFT and GOOGL report that evening.
A strong print backs the Fed's hawkish lean and lifts front-end yields. The bond market would only welcome a miss if PCE also came in soft.

economic_data.expected: Core +0.3% m/m, 3.1% y/y; headline +0.5% m/m, 3.6% y/y
economic_data.takeaway: This is the key print for duration. Core at 0.4% or more would likely push the 10Y back above 5.1% and firm up December hike odds. Core at 0.2% would let the recent bond rally continue. Headline will be lifted by energy either way.
Wage growth easing would ease fears of a wage-price spiral from oil. A hot number would confirm the Fed's worry about inflation expectations.

earnings.result: EPS $4.68 vs $4.50 est; revenue $20.06B, slightly below estimates; ~5% workforce cut announced.
earnings.takeaway: An EPS beat helped by cost cuts while revenue slips is a late-cycle signal about consumer spending. Shares fell ~3% and helped drag XLF down 1.32%. It sets a cautious tone for Visa (Tue) and Mastercard (Thu).

earnings.result: Adj. EPS $0.64 vs $0.62 est; revenue $9.45B vs $9.27B.
earnings.takeaway: A clean beat on both lines. It is early evidence that high oil prices are reaching service-company revenue and supports the XLE idea ahead of the majors.

earnings.timing: Wed 28 Oct after close (same day as FOMC)
earnings.result: Bar: EPS $4.71 vs $4.13 a year ago.
earnings.takeaway: Investors care most about Azure growth and capex guidance. With semis down 12% in a month on capex worries (n101), a capex cut would hit the chip suppliers and a capex raise would revive 'AI spending ROI' doubts. Either way it moves the Nasdaq.

earnings.result: Bar: EPS $2.94 vs $2.87 a year ago (a low growth bar).
earnings.takeaway: EPS is expected to barely grow, so cloud growth and capex will drive the reaction. Together with MSFT this is the most index-relevant event of the week after the Fed.

earnings.timing: Thu 29 Oct after close (same day as GDP/PCE)
earnings.result: Bar: EPS $2.01 vs $1.95 a year ago.
earnings.takeaway: This doubles as a read on the consumer at sentiment of 48 and on AWS capex. A weak retail outlook would confirm the AXP signal for discretionary stocks (XLY).
Estimates have already more than doubled, so a beat is expected. Buybacks and guidance at $110+ Brent will decide whether XLE, now at record highs, can go higher.

earnings.result: Bar: EPS $12.02 vs $2.52 a year ago.
earnings.takeaway: Refining margins are huge, with fuel oil above crude prices in Asia (n103). This is the first big energy report of the week and a test of how high expectations have run.

earnings.takeaway: Payment volumes give a near-real-time read on the consumer after AXP's revenue miss.

sections.summary: Stocks lost ground for a second week. The rotation that had favoured defensives for a month reversed on Friday: staples, health care and industrials sold off while chips bounced off a 12% monthly drawdown. Earnings have beaten, but by less than usual (83% beat, aggregate surprise only 2.1%). This week the Fed, PCE and three mega-caps land within 30 hours of each other, so expect gap risk rather than trend.
key_points: 1-month: SMH −12.2%, XLK −5.9%, Nasdaq −3.65% vs XLE +10.8%, XLU +8.1%, XLP +8.0%; VIX 19.45 (+24% in a month).
Friday movers: CrowdStrike +8.25%, Crown Castle +9.06% (SpaceX tower-access talks), Comfort Systems −9.26%; AXP −3% on a revenue miss and job cuts.
Concerns over memory chips and TSMC capex (n67, n101) are the overhang into MSFT and GOOGL on Wednesday and AMZN on Thursday.

sections.summary: Treasuries rallied on the week despite $117 oil: the 10Y fell 11bp to ~4.99% and the 30Y fell 12bp to 5.32%. That tells me the market is weighing growth damage more heavily than the inflation impulse. The curve is moderately steep (2s10s +31bp, 3m10y +78bp) and bills still pay ~4.2%. A hawkish hold is fully expected Wednesday, so the real test for duration is Thursday's core PCE.
key_points: Treasury par curve 23 Oct: 3M 4.22%, 2Y 4.69%, 5Y 4.82%, 10Y 5.00%, 30Y 5.33%; Friday's moves were +4bp from 2Y out.
Fed funds 3.75-4.00% after September's hike; Reuters poll 94/100 expect a hold, CME ~10% hike odds; Pimco sees a December hike.
Credit is calm but not cheering: HYG −1.1% and LQD +0.7% over the month. Evercore has published yield and spread thresholds it sees as AI-correction triggers (n151).

Supply has eased as AI companies step back from debt issuance (n60). Monday brings a 2Y auction ($69B per TBAC, not officially confirmed) and a 20-30Y buyback. French yields at a 24-year high (n28) are a source of global contagion risk.

sections.summary: Brent settled at $116.72, its highest since 29 April and a third straight weekly gain (+6.2%). The drivers were Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, Saudi supply at a three-decade low and a record month of Hormuz ship attacks. Over the weekend Trump said strikes on Iran could come at any moment, while Fujairah resumed loadings. Risk premium is likely to stay high into Monday's open. The big downside risk is a Hormuz reopening, which would release OPEC+ barrels the group has already agreed to add, plus UAE output growing after its OPEC exit.
key_points: Front-month Brent settled at $116.72 (+$3.55); the snapshot's $111.70 is most likely the next contract, which implies steep backwardation. WTI is at $103.27.
Supply: Saudi output at a 30+ year low (IEA, n164); 28 Hormuz ship attacks in October (n132); record tanker rates (n82).
Bearish offsets: OPEC+ will lift output once Hormuz reopens (n159); UAE output near record after leaving OPEC (n167); OPEC halved its 2026 demand-growth forecast (n137).
XLE and peer ETFs hit record highs on inflows (n141). The OPEC+ meeting is 1 Nov; majors report Wed to Fri.

sections.summary: BTC is holding its ~$80K cost-basis area (n2) inside a 30-day range that has narrowed to $80-86K (n29), but it dipped to ~$79,280 Saturday amid $436M of liquidations, mostly longs. ETF demand is fading at the margin: spot BTC ETFs lost $773M over Thursday and Friday, though the week was net +$301M. ETH ETFs are on track for their worst month of the year at about −$955M. Alt L1s are falling faster: AVAX −10.9%, ADA −8.2%, SUI −8.1% and TON −7.9% on the week. BNB (+2.0%) and XRP, helped by ETF inflows (n10), are the exceptions.
key_points: Spot BTC ETF flows: −$137.9M Fri (provisional), −$635.6M Thu. ETH ETFs −$220.7M on the week; headline figures vary (n31, n134).
ETH's Hoodi testnet upgrade has been postponed with no new date, and Maelstrom closed its directional ETH positions. SOL's Alpenglow upgrade is live, but SOL ETFs saw −$17.3M of outflows.
The Fed is the macro swing factor (n15, n35). The Initia exploit (about $2.7M drained) is a reminder of small-L1 risk.

brief.instructor_take: Here's what I think matters this week. An oil shock is hitting a Fed that is still in tightening mode and a consumer that already feels terrible. Last week the bond market chose to worry about growth: the 10Y fell 11bp while Brent rose 6%. The crowd reads $117 oil as an inflation story, but the market is treating it as a tax on spending. A less experienced investor might see staples and utilities up 8% in a month and assume "defensive" is safe. Friday showed how crowded that trade has become: XLP fell 1.9% on a day the Nasdaq was nearly flat. Wednesday and Thursday stack FOMC, Microsoft, Alphabet, GDP, core PCE and Amazon into about 30 hours. When the event risk is that concentrated, the right move is to set up before it and act after it, not to predict outcomes. So I want three things: cash earning 4.2% in bills, ready to deploy after PCE; a measured position in oil producers as a hedge against the very shock that hurts everything else I own; and no new money in the weakest corner of crypto. I could be wrong in two clear ways. A credible Hormuz reopening would knock $15-20 off Brent quickly, and a soft core PCE with a Fed that sounds less hawkish than feared would make me wish I'd bought duration and beaten-up semis earlier. I'll accept the cost of being late in exchange for not guessing on a binary week.

top_ideas.title: Park dry powder in T-bills through Fed/PCE week
top_ideas.one_liner: Earn ~4.2% in bills; deploy after PCE, not before
top_ideas.thesis: Bills yield about 4.2% (3M par) with essentially no duration risk, and this week puts the Fed, core PCE and three mega-cap reports inside 30 hours. Holding cash in SGOV keeps you paid while you wait and leaves the option to extend into IEF or buy equities after the data, at better-informed prices.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with what the market already prices: a hold at 3.75-4.00% with a hawkish tilt and roughly 10% odds of a hike. That means the surprise risk sits in the tone and in Thursday's core PCE, consensus 0.3% m/m. The UMich survey just showed 1-year inflation expectations at 4.7% and 5-10-year at 3.5%, which gives Warsh cover to keep December live. That is bad for anything with duration. At the same time the 10Y has already fallen 11bp in a week to ~4.99%, so buying IEF now means buying after a rally and right before the riskiest print. SGOV earns nearly as much as the 2Y (4.69%) with none of the price risk, so the cost of waiting is close to zero. The concept is option value: cash in bills is a free option to act after the uncertainty resolves. Two things would change my mind. A statement that opens the door to cuts, or a 10Y above 5.15% after PCE, would both make me move part of this into IEF.

top_ideas.title: Own the oil shock through producers, not futures
top_ideas.one_liner: Half into XLE Monday if ≤$70.50; rest on dip or after XOM/CVX
top_ideas.thesis: Brent at $116.72 with Saudi supply at a three-decade low and Hormuz attacks at a record means producers are earning windfall cash flows. Their share prices discount a much lower long-term oil price than spot. XLE gets five big earnings catalysts this week and does well in exactly the scenario that hurts the rest of a portfolio.
top_ideas.reasoning: The evidence chain runs like this. Supply is impaired (Saudi output at a 30-year low per the IEA, 28 ship attacks in Hormuz this month, record tanker rates), and Trump's weekend strike threat keeps the risk premium alive into Monday. That flows straight into producer earnings. Estimates already show it: XOM $3.96 vs $1.88 a year ago, CVX $4.78 vs $1.85, PSX $12.02 vs $2.52. SLB's beat on Friday is early confirmation. I prefer XLE to BNO because equity holders get paid through buybacks and dividends, and the stocks price in normalised oil, so they fall less if Brent drops. BNO's 14.8% monthly gain versus XLE's 10.8% shows how much more violently the futures move. The trap here is that XLE is at record highs with heavy inflows (n141), so 'beat and sell' is a real risk on Friday. That's why I split the entry and won't chase a weekend-headline gap. I'm wrong if Hormuz reopens: OPEC+ has pre-agreed extra barrels and the UAE is expanding, which could take Brent below $100 in a hurry.
catalysts: Mon open: reaction to weekend Iran strike threats
risks: Hormuz reopening or a US-Iran deal triggers a fast $15-20 drop in Brent
Crowded positioning: XLE at record highs on inflows, so beats may be sold
Demand destruction: OPEC has halved its 2026 demand-growth forecast
top_ideas.entry: Buy half Monday if XLE opens at or below ~$70.50 (Friday close $69.33). If it gaps higher on strike news, wait. Add the second half on a pullback toward $67 or after XOM and CVX report Friday.
top_ideas.invalidation: XLE closes below $65.50, or front-month Brent settles below $100 on de-escalation or Hormuz reopening news.
top_ideas.sizing: 3-4% of portfolio in total, entered in two halves

top_ideas.title: Stay out of ETH and alt L1s until flows turn
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH ETF outflows ~$955M in Oct; don't average down
top_ideas.thesis: ETH is down 14% in a month to $2,340. Spot ETH ETFs are heading for their worst month of the year at about −$955M, and the next upgrade milestone just slipped. Alt L1s are falling faster than BTC. Until institutional flows turn, any bounce is something to sell into, not a reason to buy.
top_ideas.reasoning: In crypto I follow flows first, because without earnings the marginal buyer sets the price. For ETH that buyer has been leaving: −$220.7M from ETFs last week and roughly −$955M month to date, and Maelstrom closed its directional ETH book. The fundamental story also hit a setback when developers postponed the Hoodi testnet upgrade with no new date. That delays the next upgrade narrative and removes a reason for fresh buyers to step in. This is relative strength at work. BTC is holding its ~$80K cost basis inside a tightening range, while ETH, SOL, AVAX, ADA and SUI keep making lower lows. Weak names in a weak tape tend to stay weak. A less experienced investor sees '65% off the high' on SOL or a cheap-looking ETH and buys. But price falling doesn't make something cheap when the people who were buying have stopped. A hawkish Fed on Wednesday would hit the most speculative assets first. I'll change my mind if ETH reclaims $2,700 with three or more straight days of net ETF inflows.

top_ideas.entry: No new buying. If you already hold ETH or alt L1s, don't average down; consider trimming bounces toward $2,500.
top_ideas.invalidation: ETH reclaims $2,700 with three or more consecutive days of net spot ETH ETF inflows.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new exposure; trim existing alt-L1 holdings to no more than 1-2% of portfolio

lesson.explanation: A futures curve is in backwardation when near-dated contracts cost more than later ones. That usually means barrels are scarce right now and the market expects the shortage to ease. It shows how much of today's price is an emergency premium rather than a lasting new level. It also matters for what you own: a futures fund like BNO earns a roll gain in backwardation because it keeps selling the expensive near contract and buying the cheaper next one. But when the premium collapses, the near contract falls fastest.
lesson.todays_example: Front-month Brent settled at $116.72 Friday, but the snapshot's BZ=F quote of $111.70 (likely the next contract) is about $5 lower, a steep one-month backwardation. That is why the two figures conflict. It is also why I prefer XLE: producer stocks are valued on the cheaper long-dated part of the curve, so a Hormuz reopening would hurt them less than BNO.
